verdictSummary: The core loop is small: take a file and a caption, push it to each network's upload endpoint, queue it if it is scheduled, log the result. For networks that hand out credentials on signup, like Bluesky, Mastodon and Telegram, a coding agent builds that in a sitting. What Upload-Post sells is the rest: one API key that already posts to TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, Facebook, X, Threads, Pinterest, Reddit and Google Business Profile. Those APIs sit behind Meta App Review, TikTok's audit before an app may post publicly, YouTube's upload quota and business verification, and each platform enforces its own video container, codec, aspect ratio, duration and size rules. You can vibecode a personal posting API for the open networks; you cannot vibecode the approvals or the per-platform upload handling.
coreLoopDIY: A small HTTP endpoint that takes a media file and caption and publishes or schedules it to open-API networks through per-network adapters, with a queue and an upload log.
requirements: ffmpeg for checking video against per-network limits
whatYouLose: pre-approved OAuth apps for TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, Threads, Pinterest, LinkedIn and Google Business Profile
one request format and one API key across all of those networks instead of one integration per platform
server-side FFmpeg processing and per-platform video format handling
the hosted MCP server, SDKs and n8n, Zapier and Make integrations for agent and no-code posting
token refresh and the steady patching as platform APIs change
moatNotes: platform app review + video handling + integration upkeep
whyPeopleStillPay: Posting to Instagram, TikTok or YouTube from your own code normally means registering a developer app per platform and getting it through review and business verification, which takes weeks and which a solo developer often cannot qualify for. Upload-Post's OAuth apps are already approved, so a user connects an account and your code sends one request with one API key. The subscription also covers the upkeep: expiring tokens, per-platform media rules, and endpoints that change on someone else's schedule. Developers building agents or automations pay for that layer, plus the hosted MCP server and the n8n, Zapier and Make integrations, rather than maintaining ten integrations themselves.

notes: Same shape as the other schedulers, sold as an API first · the code is a weekend, the platform approvals and upload handling behind it are not.
prompt:
Build me a personal social posting API to replace Upload-Post. Requirements:

- Node + Express + better-sqlite3 on my always-on box. One POST /upload endpoint
  that takes a video, image or text post plus caption, a list of target networks,
  and an optional scheduled_date; a GET /history endpoint for the last 100 uploads.
- Auth with a single API key from .env sent as an Authorization header. Bind to
  localhost only; no accounts, no telemetry.
- Open-API networks only: Bluesky (app password via @atproto/api), Mastodon (access
  token), and a Telegram channel (bot token). One adapter file per network, creds in
  .env, so a fourth network is one new file.
- For the gated platforms (TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, Threads, LinkedIn,
  Pinterest, Google Business Profile) do not fight the APIs: return a clear
  "not supported" per network and say in the README that these need reviewed
  developer apps and business verification, not more code.
- Scheduled uploads go in a queue table; a node-cron tick every minute sends what is
  due, marks the row sending before it calls anything so a crash never double-posts,
  retries 3 times with backoff, then records sent or failed with the error and the
  live post URL.
- Media stored in media/ beside the database. Images resized per network with sharp.
  Video: MP4 only, checked with ffprobe against each network's duration and size
  limits at request time and rejected with the limit in the message.
- Out of scope: video transcoding, analytics, comments, DMs, and multi-user profiles.
- README: getting each credential, a curl example per endpoint, and a warning that
  social APIs drift and need patching.
